Basal metabolic rate measurements obtained from respirometry trials indicate that the Mauritian tomb bat (Taphozous mauritianus) sustains a resting oxygen consumption of 31.14 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 31.14 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when measured at 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], a temperature close to typical deep-body thermoneutral conditions for this species. Newborn pups are remarkably small relative to adult dimensions, with a neonatal wet weight at birth estimated at 5.5 grams [Wwb = 5.5 grams], a value derived from measurements of the congener Taphozous longimanus and consistent with the altricial developmental pattern observed across emballonurid bats. This modest birth mass imposes substantial energetic demands on lactating females during the early postnatal period.

The ultimate wet weight for adult females of this species typically stabilizes around 30 grams [Wwi = around 30 grams], based on field measurements ranging from 27.5 to 31.6 grams, whereas adult males attain a slightly higher maximum recorded body mass of approximately 32 grams [Wwi = approximately 32 grams] following a broader reported range of 20 to 36 grams. This degree of sexual size dimorphism, though modest, may reflect divergent energetic strategies between the sexes, with males investing in sustained flight activity for territory defense while females allocate resources toward gestation and lactation.

Reproductive output in T. mauritianus is constrained by a slow life-history pace. Under standard thermal conditions of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], females typically produce a single pup per litter [N_R_i = single pup per litter] and complete roughly one litter per year [F_R_i = roughly one litter per year], corresponding to a low maximum reproductive rate that is characteristic of tropical bat species with extended parental care. Gestation time, based on data from the related species Taphozous longimanus, lasts approximately 60 days [tg = approximately 60 days] when females are maintained at a body temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], reflecting the prolonged embryogenesis typical of small, altricial mammals.

The duration of lactation dependency is relatively brief compared to the total pre-reproductive phase. Onset of weaning, marked by the transition from exclusive milk ingestion to solid food consumption, occurs at about 37 days after birth [tx = about 37 days after birth] under standard thermal conditions of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], a timing that aligns with the rapid wing development observed in emballonurids. Following nutritional independence, the sub-adult phase extends considerably before gonadal maturation is achieved; puberty is attained at 278 days since birth [tp = 278 days since birth] when measured at 38.5 °C [T = 38.5 °C], indicating that reproductive competence requires nearly ten months of post-weaning growth and physiological development.

Maximum recorded longevity estimates, extrapolated from long-term marking studies of T. longimanus, suggest that the Mauritian tomb bat can live up to approximately 4 years [am = approximately 4 years] under conditions approximating 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C]. This lifespan, while modest compared to some larger-bodied tropical bats, represents a substantial investment in somatic durability relative to similarly sized insectivorous mammals. The combination of a protracted juvenile period, low annual fecundity, and moderate adult survival places T. mauritianus firmly within the slow end of the mammalian life-history continuum, a strategy that likely buffers populations against environmental stochasticity in their island habitats across the western Indian Ocean.
